**The file will not open.**
Solidon says what is wrong with it: empty, cut off, not an STL or 3MF despite the extension, zero triangles or no extent. Usually the download broke off, or a server's error page arrived instead of the model; with zero triangles, nothing was selected when exporting. *Choose another file* leads straight to the file selection.

**The model has openings.**
Solidon repairs what it safely can while importing, and the report says so, for example “One hole was closed.” A large opening gets a new surface, with *Show the place* and *Leave open* below it. If something stays open, it says for example “One open place could not be closed safely.”, and *Show the places* leads there. If a whole wall is missing, another source is the shorter way.

**Combining or subtracting fails or removes too much.**
Both need clean bodies. Solidon tries several methods and says which one worked; if it had to compute on a grid, precision was lost. Then repair first and try again. If the report says “Parts of the model overlap.”, the button *Resolve overlaps* helps. If two faces lie exactly on top of each other, let the body to be subtracted stick out by a hundredth of a millimetre; parts do that by themselves.

**The part does not fit the bed.**
*Split automatically* cuts it into pieces that fit ([When the part does not fit the bed](manual:splitting)). Check the build volume in the printer profile too.

**The fit is too tight or too loose.**
Do not change the model; measure and enter the value under *Calibrate material* ([Trying instead of guessing: variants and calibration](manual:variants)).

**A step can no longer be changed.**
If the change would alter the number of objects that later steps work with, the evaluation stops. Undo the later steps, make the change and build them again.

**STEP is greyed out.**
STEP needs individually editable faces and edges. For a triangle mesh, choose *Convert to faces and edges*. Then check the shape and the report: conversion does not automatically restore the original CAD construction. You can also switch an existing basic-shape step to *Compute with true faces and edges* through its context menu in the history. Fillet and chamfer also work on meshes.

**The actions on the right are locked.**
If the chain stops at a step, for example because a part fits no bed, Solidon accepts no new step after it, because it would never be computed. Each button explains why it is unavailable, and the report offers the next step.

**The chat does not answer.**
It needs a key of your own or a local Ollama ([The chat](manual:chat)).

**Everything is sluggish.**
While you work, Solidon uses draft quality; it computes the final detail for export. With very detailed models, simplifying early helps; the triangle count is in the object tree. On opening, a loading indicator shows that the project is still loading.

**A grey button says why it is grey**, as a tooltip, in the status line and for the screen reader. Without a reason, it is a bug in Solidon.

**Every error message should offer a next step.** If no action to continue is offered, that is a bug in Solidon and worth a report: *Help → Send feedback*. The preview shows what will be included: a screenshot, the log and, if you choose, the session. If you do not want to hand anything over, save a folder on your own computer instead.

For the print file and the cross-check from the G-code. PrusaSlicer, SuperSlicer, OrcaSlicer, ElegooSlicer, Bambu Studio, Creality Print, Anycubic Slicer Next and Cura are recognised. On first start, Solidon suggests the printer the slicer last used.

## Ollama for the chat without a key of your own

Ollama comes without a model and is not necessarily running. *Edit → Set up the chat* takes care of both:

1. **Is it running?** The dialog says so, and a button starts it. If it runs on another computer, its address belongs in the list of optional programs.
2. **Fetch a model.** The choice lists the installed ones and the proven ones. *Fetch the model* downloads seven to nineteen gigabytes; an interrupted download resumes later.
3. **Check tools.** Only a test with a real request shows whether a model actually calls tools. If the chat answers but carries nothing out, a different model helps.

**The test also measures the speed** and says how long it takes until an answer starts. Without a graphics card, Ollama computes on the processor, orders of magnitude slower; if the wait shown is minutes, the local route is not worth it on this computer. After ten minutes Solidon cancels a local request.

**A model that fits entirely into graphics memory usually responds faster.** Parameter count alone does not establish reliable tool calls; run the tool test for your model. Models that have performed well are listed in [Which models Solidon uses](manual:models). For long exchanges, a key for a hosted model is worth it. Ollama itself supports AMD cards via **ROCm**; **IPEX-LLM** and **OpenVINO** are separate installations that Solidon does not set up; the tool test shows whether such a route holds up.

## ComfyUI for generating from text or an image

ComfyUI needs the nodes the workflow addresses and the model for them. Solidon puts both in place, via *Set up nodes and model …* in the ComfyUI row or straight from *File → Generate model* when ComfyUI is running there without the nodes. Solidon finds the **desktop version** from comfy.org by itself; for the portable one, point it at the folder with `custom_nodes` and `main.py` if needed.

The setup fetches the pinned TripoSG source code, installs missing packages and **checks that ComfyUI can load the nodes**. On request, the model follows with about 7.5 GB and, for the route from text, the image model with about 6.9 GB. An interrupted run resumes where it stopped. **Then restart ComfyUI once**, otherwise *Generate model* stays greyed out. During a generation Solidon shows the elapsed time; if something breaks off, ComfyUI's message is shown in the dialog.

*File → Hand over to the slicer* (Ctrl+P) leads from the model to the print file. The slicer computes it, but it is operated from here, usually without you seeing it. [Check and print a model](manual:print-a-model) shows it step by step.

**At the front are the values you change on every part:** infill density and supports; layer height, walls, temperatures and the search sit under *More settings*. Every field says in one sentence what it does. What the geometry calls for, the analysis suggests with a reason, for example supports under the measured overhang or a minimum time per layer for a part that tapers to a point. If you choose brim, skirt or raft under *Adhesion*, only the settings of that bed type appear there. A number outside its limit stays in the field, the limit is shown next to it, and *Slice* waits until it is right.

**Where the values come from:** With PrusaSlicer and the Orca family (OrcaSlicer, Bambu Studio, ElegooSlicer, Creality Print, Anycubic Slicer Next), printer, process and filament come from the slicer, and Solidon only adds your changes and accepted suggestions on top; if the Orca family lacks a profile, the status line says which. The quality picks the manufacturer's process, and a choice of your own stays. With Cura, Solidon takes over the printer Cura is currently using if you ask it to, with its nozzle and start and end code. The other print settings on this route are based on Solidon's tables, supplemented by your changes and accepted suggestions.

**Slice** lets the slicer compute and reads the print file back: print time, material and layers then appear in the dialog and in the report, marked as coming from the G-code and kept apart from Solidon's estimate and a weighed remaining amount. *Save print file* stores the G-code, with several plates one file per plate.

Parts are shared as files, using whichever transfer method you choose. Solidon has no public library, uploads nothing and needs neither an account nor a network. The file ends in `.solidon-part` and carries the Solidon icon.

**Sharing a part:** in the part catalogue (*File → Part catalogue …*, Ctrl+K), select a part of your own and press *Share part as a file …*. The file carries author and licence. Supplied and imported parts keep their origin; saving again does not make someone else's work yours.

**The licence is spelled out:** *Public domain — anyone may do anything, no conditions*, *Attribution — my name must be credited* or *Attribution, and adaptations under the same licence*. The third one requires others to pass on their improvement in the same way. The name next to it is freely chosen; initials are enough.

**The file carries data, never executable source code:** the recipe of steps and values and, where needed, embedded model data. Solidon checks size, structure and integrity both when sharing and when importing.

**Importing a part:** in the catalogue, choose *Add part from a file …*. If validation succeeds, the part appears in the catalogue and works like any other. If it fails, Solidon identifies the missing field, invalid value or unknown operation. If it has the same name as one of your own, yours stays and the new one gets a derived name.

**An imported part stays in the catalogue**, its origin visible. With CC BY, every shared copy names the original author; with CC BY-SA, a derived version must also be released under the same licence.

Everything stays offline. Neither the file nor its author, licence or origin is sent to RS Digital.

Das Stück, das Solidon von einem Slicer:
The piece that sets Solidon apart from a slicer. A printed part is never as large as drawn: plastic shrinks, a 5 mm hole comes out narrower, the bottom layer is squashed wider. If two parts are to fit into each other, that has to be allowed for, and Solidon does it for you.

**The clearance lives in the material profile, not in the model.** To put a pin into a hole, you do not enter 0.2 but choose a *Fit*; the number comes from the profile of the material you print with.

![](figure:fit)

**That is why a calibration works backwards.** A value under *Edit → Calibrate material* applies to every fit, including those in projects made earlier. It is measured on a printed test piece, as described in [Trying instead of guessing: variants and calibration](manual:variants).

**The first layer is a special case.** It is pressed against the bed and spreads outwards: the elephant foot. For a fit at the bottom of the part, it decides whether it goes in.

![](figure:elephant-foot)

**The test piece** cuts a cube around one spot out of the part instead of rebuilding it: the real shape with the same tolerance, as a small section for a test print.

**A scene may have several materials.** A TPU seal in a PETG enclosure shrinks differently and wants more clearance. *Set material* gives a body its own profile, and tolerances, elephant foot and fit check calculate with it.

The chat calls the same operations as the window. It chooses operations and values; the program does the computing.

**How it goes:** you write what you want and get a proposal, a list of operations not yet carried out. The view shows in blue what would be added and in orange what would disappear. *Apply* enters it into the history as one transaction, one Ctrl+Z takes it back completely, and *Discard* leaves nothing behind.

**It sees a digest:** dimensions, recognised features, project parameters, selection and report. After a Ctrl+Z its contribution counts as discarded.

**It needs a language model**, either a key of your own (*Edit → Set up the chat*, stored in the system keychain, never in the project file) or a local Ollama ([Setting up optional programs](manual:extras)). Without a model only the chat is greyed out, and it says why.

The holder for the workbench took an evening. Next time it should be an entry in the catalogue, with an adjustable width, because the next board is thicker.

**Project parameters first.** Exactly what has a name in the project becomes adjustable. If you wrote the width into the box as a fixed number, you get a part with exactly one width. Create the values as parameters beforehand and tie the dimensions to them ([Parameters and expressions](manual:parameters)).

**Then choose in the history what goes along**, with Ctrl or Shift; with no selection the whole history counts, which is the common case. In the part catalogue (*File → Part catalogue …*, Ctrl+K) you find *Save selection as a part …*. The button stays locked while parameters are missing and says what is missing. At the top, the dialog names the steps it received.

![](figure:own-part)

**The dialog asks five things:** the name in the catalogue, the group, a description, for every parameter whether and how it can be adjusted (label, unit, limits, default and a sentence on what it does), and for every recognised feature whether it can be clicked later, say a hole for aligning. Without at least one exposed dimension and one exposed spot, *Create part* stays locked.

**Creating it computes:** the part is built once at every corner of the given range, smallest width with greatest height and so on. If even one corner yields no usable body, the catalogue entry says so before you use it.

**It stays on this computer** and is marked next to the supplied parts; nothing is uploaded. If you pass on a project that uses it, it travels along as a recipe, a list of steps and values, not a program. If the recipient already has a part of that name, theirs wins, and the one that came along gets its own.

**Changing means saving again** under the same name; the button is then called *Replace part*. If the project is gone or the part came as a file, *Open for editing …* brings its steps back into the history together with what you entered. An imported part stays marked as imported.

**Every recipe has a version** that follows from its content. If a project uses an older one, Solidon says so on opening; the old version travels in the project, appears as an entry of its own in the catalogue, and you decide which applies.

Die Wörter, die in Solidon, in Slicern u:
The words that turn up in Solidon, in slicers and in printing forums — briefly explained.

**Mesh** — a body as a shell of triangles. STL and OBJ contain nothing else: no circles, no dimensions, only triangles.

**Closed (watertight)** — the shell has no hole, inside and outside are unambiguous. Only a closed body can be combined and printed reliably.

**Feature** — a place in the mesh where Solidon has recognised a known shape: a hole, a peg, a rounding, a face. Ten thousand triangles turn back into something you can click on and change.

**Operation** — one working step: drilling, filleting, splitting, placing a part. In Solidon, geometry comes about this way and no other.

**Transaction** — everything one undo takes back at once. A proposal from the chat is exactly one, even when it consists of five operations.

**Parameter** — a named dimension of the project, `width` for instance. Operations may compute with it; when the value changes, everything hanging on it changes.

**Part** — a ready-made construction element from the library, with dimensions from a table rather than from memory.

**Sketch (drawing)** — a flat outline of lines, circles and arcs. A body is made from it, and it stays editable afterwards: moving a line means changing the part.

**Constraint** — a rule that holds the drawing together: two lines parallel, a distance fixed, one point on another. When something is dragged, they keep holding.

**Degree of freedom** — what can still move in a drawing. “4 more dimensions and nothing can move” means: four things are not yet settled. At zero the drawing is fully defined.

**Fully defined** — every number of the drawing is given, nothing shifts any more. Not fully defined does not mean wrong: the drawing works, it can just still be moved.

**Extrude (pull up)** — raising an outline perpendicular to its plane until a body comes out of it. The usual way from drawing to part; under *Create → Draw* this kind is called *Extrude base shape*, and other programs call it extruding.

**Pocket** — the same inwards: the outline is cut out of an existing body instead of a new one being set on top.

**Profile** — the closed outline a body is made from. Not the same as the material or printer profile, which supplies values.

**Curve** — a smooth line through several placed points, for shapes that are neither straight nor circular. Other design programs call it a spline.

**Guide line** — a line that carries constraints but forms no body itself. The centre line something hangs on symmetrically is not meant to be printed too.

**Fit** — how tightly two parts sit inside one another. The clearance needed comes from the material profile.

**Clearance** — the gap between peg and hole so that the two can be joined. Too little jams, too much wobbles.

**Press fit** — interference instead of clearance: the part is pressed in and holds by itself.

**Tolerance** — the amount by which a dimension deliberately departs from the nominal size so that the printed result comes out right.

**Shrinkage** — plastic contracts as it cools. That is why a printed part is slightly smaller than drawn.

**Elephant foot** — the lowest layer is pressed against the bed and spreads outwards. The part is wider at the bottom than planned.

**Overhang** — a face growing outwards at an angle. Beyond a certain angle the layer below has nothing left to rest on.

**Supports** — material printed under an overhang and broken off afterwards.

**Island** — an area of a layer with nothing underneath it. Without a support the printer prints into thin air there.

**Bridge (span)** — a horizontal run between two points of support. Short bridges succeed without support, long ones sag.

**Nozzle** — the opening the plastic comes out of, usually 0.4 mm. It limits how fine a detail can be.

**Line width** — how wide the nozzle lays a line. For filament printing, Solidon uses two adjacent lines as a guideline for minimum wall thickness.

**Layer height** — how thick one layer is, usually 0.2 mm. Smaller means finer and slower.

**Slicer** — the program that turns the model into the print file. Solidon is not one and replaces none.

**G-code** — the finished list of instructions for the printer. It comes out of the slicer.

**STL** — the most widespread format: triangles only, no unit, no colour.

**3MF** — the modern successor: with unit, colours and several objects in one file. Wherever the slicer can read it, it is the better choice.

**STEP** — a format with real faces and edges instead of triangles. What classical CAD programs exchange.

**GLB** — the format of the viewers: triangles with colours, in a single file that every browser opens. Meant for showing, not for printing.

**Report** — the list of what stands out about the scene, each entry with an action that fixes it.

**Filament** — a named spool with a colour and print settings of its own. In multi-colour printing it is assigned to a whole part or to a recognised face.

Die Zahl, die über eine Passung entschei:
The number that decides a fit is the clearance, and it depends on printer, material and nozzle. It is guessed once, then measured.

**It is measured on a printed test body.** In the part catalogue (*File → Part catalogue …*, `Ctrl+K`), under *Calibration*, you find the *Fit test body*: pegs and holes with graded clearance, by default four steps from 0.10 to 0.25 mm, changeable in the dialog. Print it once, try the pairs and take the value that fits snugly.

![](figure:part-fit-ladder)

**The value belongs in the material profile:** *Edit → Calibrate material*. Every tolerance is a reference to it, so afterwards last week's lid fits better too, without anyone touching it.

**The same for walls and overhangs:** *Wall thickness ladder* and *Overhang fan* measure the thinnest wall that holds and the angle from which this printer needs supports. Until then, the angle from the manufacturer's profile applies, 45 degrees for a generic printer.

**If a number depends on the part rather than the material**, *Edit → Generate variants* helps. It runs a project parameter through a range and lays the versions side by side, for example five handle diameters on one plate. The project stays unchanged; the variants are just an output.

The guide carries a post, a collar with detent notches, tactile marks and one opening per position; the dial carries a window, a spring hub and a detent tongue. Ein Halter aus Bausteinen mit änderbarer: A holder from parts with adjustable width, depth and thickness.

Ein Innenradius passt nicht in sein Fach: An inner radius does not fit its compartment. Reduce the radius or enlarge the compartment.
Ein Kabelclip: der Bügel auf einer Fläch: A cable clip: the bow on a face whose opening is narrower than the cable it guides.
Ein Kernloch quer durch jede Aufnahme. D: A core hole across each socket. The screw cuts its own thread and clamps the rod; without it, the rod is only pushed in.
Ein Klick auf einen Befund zeigt darunte: Click a finding to see below it what you can do.
Ein Kragen führt den abnehmbaren Deckel: A collar guides the removable lid into the opening.
Ein Kreis braucht einen Radius größer al: A circle needs a radius greater than zero.
Ein Kreis ist keine Bahn — er hat kein E: A circle is no path — it has no end for the cross-section to start at.

Ein Langloch braucht einen positiven Dur: A slot needs a positive diameter.
Ein Langloch ist ein Hohlraum und keine: A slot is a cavity, not material. Its width is changed by “Change bore”, its length and direction by “Pull into a slot”.
Ein Langloch muss deutlich länger sein a: A slot has to be noticeably longer than its diameter — otherwise it is a round hole. Enter at least the length shown below.
Ein Langloch muss länger als breit sein: A slot must be longer than it is wide — otherwise it is a circle.
Ein Langloch nimmt eine Verengung nicht: A slot does not take a narrowing along. Remove it first with “Remove feature”, or leave the hole round.
Ein Langloch und eine Aufweitung gehen n: A slot and a widening do not go together. Set the widening to zero, or leave the hole round.
Ein Lochkreis trägt höchstens vierundsec: A bolt circle carries at most sixty-four holes.
Ein Lochwand-Einhänger: Haken im Raster: A pegboard hook: hooks in the grid of a pegboard, with the springy latch tongue that clicks in behind the board.
Ein Lufteinschluss trägt kein Maß, an de: An air pocket carries no measurement by which its size or rotation could be changed — its shape lies in its faces alone; and a second cavity inside the material is not something one creates. What does work: moving it, and “Remove feature” fills it with material.
Ein Maß benennen, auf das Operationen un: Name a dimension that operations and sketches can reference as @name.
Ein Maß lässt sich nur auf etwas beziehe: A size can only refer to something that has one.
A dimension below zero does not exist.
Ein Merkmal dieser Passung gibt es nicht: A feature of this fit no longer exists, or it can no longer be recognised after a later step.
Ein Merkmal ist unter seinem Namen nicht: A feature cannot be found under its name, so the fit is missing. You can add it on the right under Selection.
Ein Merkmal wurde verworfen, weil es nic: A feature was discarded because it could not be matched.
Ein Merkmal, auf das sich eine Passung o: A feature that a fit or a later step refers to can no longer be recognised after this step.
Ein Modell wird gerade erzeugt. Schließe: A model is being generated. Closing cancels the generation.
Ein Muster auf einem runden Griff: A pattern on a round grip
Ein Muster braucht mindestens zwei Ausfe: A pattern needs at least two copies.
Ein Muster braucht mindestens zwei Eleme: A pattern needs at least two elements.
Ein Muster braucht mindestens zwei Plätz: A pattern needs at least two places.
Ein Muster braucht mindestens zwei Zelle: A pattern needs at least two cells. Select more identical features in the object tree.
Ein Muster liegt auf seiner Fläche und h: A pattern lies on its face and has its place there; the face or the body is what gets offset, turned or duplicated. “Change feature” redraws spacing, cell width and depth, “Remove feature” fills the cells.
Ein Name auf dem Deckel, eine Größe auf:
A name on the lid, a size on the drawer, a sign for the workbench. Both ways are in the *Create* menu: *Put text on* sets the lettering raised or recessed onto a face of the selected body, *Lettering as a body* creates it as an object of its own, for gluing on or for two-colour printing. A clicked face fills in position and direction by itself. With *On both sides*, the same lettering also goes on the opposite side, where the direction leaves the body again, readable from outside, on a flag for example.

**Eight fonts travel with the program**, so a project looks the same everywhere: a sans-serif, a serif and a monospaced one in two families each, plus a rounded one and a script. The six straight ones come in regular, bold, italic and bold italic, under *More settings*; the rounded one and the script only in regular. Bold stays legible where the regular weight already smears.

**Whether a font holds up is decided by the nozzle.** Solidon measures the stroke width of the text against the narrowest line your printer lays and says from which height it holds up. Nothing is locked; a sign that is only for looking at may be small.

**The letters appear in the object tree like other features**, straight sides as faces, rounded ones as *Curved face*. Both take a filament of their own: click, then *Filament on a face* on the right. Lettering keeps its filament even when it is split into letters for the bed.

**The text stays changeable.** A double-click on the step in the history reopens text, size, font and depth; a typo is corrected, not set anew.
Ein Objekt liegt außerhalb der freigegeb: An object lies outside the permitted printable area.
Ein Objekt liegt außerhalb des Druckbett: An object lies outside the build plate.
Ein Objekt passt nur mit schmalerem Rand: An object only fits on the print area with a narrower margin.
An object floats above the print bed.
An object sits below the build plate.
Ein Objekt steht über den Bauraum hinaus: An object sticks out of the build volume.
Ein Operationsdialog: vorn die zwei bis: An operation dialog: at the front the two or three values you actually change, below them the collapsed “More settings” section.
Ein Parameter ist ein benanntes Maß. Ope: A parameter is a named dimension. Operations and sketches reference it as @name, and turning the number rebuilds the model.
Ein Parameter liegt außerhalb seiner Gre: A parameter is outside its limits, but it is still used. Check the expression or the limits.
Ein Parameterausdruck lässt sich nicht a: A parameter expression cannot be resolved — until it is right, Solidon does not compute the scene.
Ein Passungspaar braucht zwei Merkmale a: A fit needs two features written as obj_1:hole_2.
Ein Profil zeichnen; was daraus wird, fr: Draw a profile; at “Done”, the dialog asks what it should become.
Ein Profilpfad enthält ein Semikolon. Di: A profile path contains a semicolon. This slicer separates its profiles with it and reads the path as two.
Ein Projekt aus einer früheren Sitzung w: A project from an earlier session was never saved.
Ein Projekt hat benannte Parameter wie `:
A project has named parameters such as `breite`, `tiefe` or `wandstaerke`, and operations calculate with them instead of fixed numbers.

**What for:** a number that stands in seven places gets changed in six and the seventh is overlooked. A parameter stands in one place. Turn `breite`, and everything that depends on it follows: the hole in the middle stays in the middle, because it says `=@breite/2` there and not “35”.

**Creating one:** on the left under *Parameters*, click *Create parameter*, enter name and value.

**Getting it into a dimension:** once the project has parameters, the **fx** button next to every number field switches it to an expression. Then the field accepts `=@breite/2`: `=` starts an expression, `@` refers to a parameter. After `@` the field suggests the names, and below it says what is allowed.

![](figure:parameter-field)

**Name and label can differ.** The list may say *Width*, the expression `@breite`. The suggestion list inserts the right one.

**Limits, unit and expression** are changed with a right-click on the parameter, *Change …*, undoable like every change. If a typed number is outside the limits, Solidon does not accept it and shows the limit underneath; *Change a parameter …* leads there.

**Allowed are** the four basic arithmetic operations, brackets, `min`, `max`, `abs`, `round` and references to other parameters, for example `=@breite/2 - @wand` or `=max(@breite, 40)`. Nothing else: Solidon computes expressions itself and executes nothing. A project file travels between people and must not be a program, even if a language model wrote the expression.

**Circular references** such as `a` pointing to `b` and `b` to `a` are recognised and named by Solidon, instead of computing forever.

Everything is calculated in millimetres and double precision, rounded only on display: what shows as “40.00 mm” is internally a number with all its digits.
Ein Projektmaß braucht endliche Zahlen —: A project dimension needs finite numbers — for the value as well as the bounds.
Ein Punkt auf der Drehachse; auf seiner: A point on the axis of rotation; the cross-section starts at its height along the axis. With a chosen feature only this height counts.
A point consists of two numbers.
Ein Punkt der Kurve selbst liegt schon a: A point of the curve itself already lies on it or defines it — it needs no constraint for that.
Ein Radius für die ganze Kante oder ein: One radius for the whole edge, or a changing radius, for a handle, say. On a mesh it cannot run over corners where an outer and an inner edge meet.
Ein Radius über die ganze Kante — die ge: One radius along the whole edge — the usual fillet.
Ein Rechtsgewinde und ein Linksgewinde g: A right-hand thread and a left-hand thread cannot engage. Select a counterpart with the same thread direction or undo the mirroring.
A right-hand and a left-hand thread do not engage. The library has no counterpart for a left-hand thread.
Ein Rechtsklick auf einen Schritt im *Ve: Right-click a step in the *History* to see what you can do with it.
Ein Resin-Drucker belichtet Schichten in:
A resin printer exposes layers in a bath of resin; there is no nozzle, no lines and no elephant foot. On first start, two resin printers appear in the same list as the filament printers, a small one like the Mars or Photon Mono and a large one like the Saturn or Photon M. You can create your own with build volume, pixel size and minimum wall.

**What is different then:** the minimum wall comes from the printer profile, the smallest detail is the pixel. The report says nothing about bridges, brim, filament changes and nozzle temperatures, and the print dialog shows only printer, material, plates and the program.

**The way to the printer is the file**, because many resin printers only work with their manufacturer's slicer. *Open in slicer* hands the file to any program, *Export* stores it. Where Solidon knows the shape exactly, it resolves it as finely as the pixels require, and the report names the size.
Ein Rezept ist ein Objekt, keine Liste u: A recipe is an object, not a list and not a number.
Ein Rezept kann höchstens {limit} Maße f: A recipe can expose at most {limit} dimensions. Remove additional dimensions from the selection.
Ein Rezeptschritt enthält unbekannte Ein: A recipe step contains unknown settings.
Ein Ring um ein Rohr mit zwei Klemmohren: A ring around a pipe with two clamping lugs and a screw across both. Tightened, it closes the gap and the ring grips. Pipe from the pipe series of the standard parts table or with a custom diameter; the clearance comes from the material profile.
Ein Ring, der der ganze Körper ist, läss: A ring that is the whole body cannot be moved, changed, turned, duplicated or removed on its own. Move the body.
Ein Rändel für den Griff, eine Wabe fürs:
A knurl for grip, a honeycomb for looks, a lattice instead of solid material: this is real geometry, not a texture in the picture. The slicer gets what you see.

**Eight patterns:** rib, wave, knurl straight and crossed, honeycomb, dimples, Voronoi and noise. Knurl gives grip, honeycomb and rib are decoration, Voronoi and noise hide the layer lines. The preview in the dialog is drawn from the same outlines that get printed.

![](figure:textures)

**Apply texture** embosses a pattern raised or recessed onto a face, and on a round part all the way around. The spacing must be wider than two nozzle lines, the depth higher than one layer; Solidon checks both beforehand, because an embossing that is too fine disappears in the print.

![](figure:texture)

**Changing a pattern:** click the textured spot, then *Change texture* on the right. Pattern, spacing, depth and rotation are there, and depending on the application also width and height. *Apply* changes the existing step; if several fit, choose the one you mean first. Ctrl+Z restores the old values.

**Fill with lattice** replaces the inside of a body with gyroid, honeycomb or cubic lattice. Unlike the slicer's infill, it belongs to the model, travels with the file and can be measured; its wall thickness is checked against the nozzle.

For this, the inner space has to be known. For a body you hollowed out yourself, it is. For an imported hollow part, Solidon temporarily closes the vent's through holes, and whatever is enclosed then counts as the inner space; the message says so. Otherwise the only way is to hollow out the body first.
Ein Rändel gehört um den Griff, nicht al: A knurl belongs around the grip, not as a patch on it.
Ein Satz: was passiert, wenn man ihn änd: One sentence: what happens when you change it
Ein Satz: wofür ist das Teil: One sentence: what the part is for
Ein Scharnier, das aus dem Drucker schon: A hinge that comes off the printer already moving: two leaves around a printed-in pin, with the print gap between them. Nothing to assemble, nothing to insert.
Ein Scharnierauge: eine Lasche mit Bohru: A hinge eye: a tab with a hole a dowel pin passes through — half of a joint that turns instead of bending.
Ein Schild mit Schrift im zweiten Filame: A hanging sign with lettering in a second filament.
Ein Schlüssel aus der Umgebung muss auße: A key from the environment must be removed outside Solidon.
A key comes from the environment.
A key is stored in the keychain.
Ein Schritt des Rezepts ist in dieser So: A step in the recipe is not known to this version of Solidon.
Ein Schritt des Rezepts scheiterte an di: A step of the recipe failed at this combination of parameters.
Ein Slicer-Profil wird über seinen Namen: Choose a slicer profile by name, not by a file path.
Ein Standfuß: ein gedruckter Fuß mit Fas: A foot: a printed foot with the chamfer facing down, so that the elephant foot of the first layer squeezes into empty space.
A stack of layers on the print bed. The lowest is wider than all the others because it is pressed down — the elephant foot.
Ein Stift braucht eine Bohrung. Wählen S: A pin needs a hole. Choose a hole on this part.
Ein Stift gehört in ein Innengewinde, di: A pin belongs in an internal thread, and this is an external thread. Choose a hole or an internal thread.
Ein T-förmiger Fuß, der von der Stirnsei: A T-shaped foot that slides into the T-slot of an aluminium extrusion from the end and holds there. Unlike a T-nut it has no thread: it belongs to the printed part and holds it in the slot without a screw. Neck and head come from the standard parts table. For printing, the tongue is best laid flat along the slot direction — standing upright, the shoulder under the head is an overhang.
Ein Teil der Oberfläche passt auf keine: Part of the surface fits no recognised face and stays flat triangles, as in the mesh.
Ein Teil der Züge hat die Fläche nicht e: Some strokes did not reach the surface, usually because the shape underneath was moved. Sculpt those spots again.
Ein Teil des Bausteins sitzt neben dem O: Some of the part sits beside the object and hangs in mid-air — printed, it would come out as loose pieces. Give it a back plate, which joins what stands beside it; or reduce the grid steps so everything moves closer together.
Some of the part sits beside the object and hangs in the air — printed, there would be loose pieces. Attach the part to a feature of the object or move its position closer.
Ein Teil des Modells ist eine Fläche ohn: Part of the model is a surface without thickness.
Ein Teil ist größer als die Druckfläche,: A part is too large for the print area, even when rotated.
Ein Teil ist höher, als dieser Drucker d: A part is taller than this printer can print.
Ein Teil liegt ganz in einem anderen. Sl: One part lies entirely inside another. Depending on their settings, slicers print it hollow or solid.
Ein Teil, das nicht auf das Bett passt,: Split an oversized part into pieces with pins and arrange them on the print bed.
Ein Textfeld der Quellenherkunft ist ung: A text field in the source provenance is invalid.
A change to the history is still running.
Ein Vektor einer Merkmalszuordnung ist u: A vector of a feature mapping is invalid.
Ein Verschluss zum Einsetzen und Drehen:: A closure you insert and turn: the socket has L-slots through its wall, the collar the matching lugs. Insert axially, turn through the turn angle, and at the end of the slot the lug stops. Place both halves with the same dimensions.
Ein Verweis folgt seinem Merkmal, das je: A reference follows its feature, which now has a different name.
Ein Verweis verlöre sein Merkmal — geänd: A reference would lose its feature — nothing was changed.
Ein Verweis wurde auf ein anderes Merkma: A reference was rewritten to another feature.
Ein Verweis zeigt auf ein Merkmal, das e: A reference points at a feature that no longer exists.
Ein Vieleck braucht zwischen drei und vi: A polygon needs between three and sixty-four corners.
Ein Vorschlag nimmt entweder zurück oder: A proposal either undoes or adds — doing both in one go could not be undone completely.
Ein Vorschlag nimmt genau eine zurück —: One proposal undoes exactly one — another one needs its own turn.
Ein Wert darin ist keine endliche Zahl o: A value in it is not a finite number or exceeds what a project file can hold. Check parameters with bounds such as infinity, then save again.
Ein Wert liegt außerhalb des zulässigen: A value is outside the allowed range.
Ein Wert sieht aus wie ein Dateipfad — ü: A value looks like a file path — this interface does not accept that.
Ein Wiederholen holt diesen Schritt zurü: A redo brings this step back.
Ein Winkelmaß liegt zwischen null und 18: An angle dimension lies between zero and 180 degrees.
Ein Zehntel Verengung am Rand, damit der: A tenth of a millimetre narrower at the rim so the magnet cannot fall out.
Ein Ziel besteht aus dem Objekt und dem: A target consists of the object and the feature, separated by a colon — for example obj_2:hole_1.
Ein Zug auf der Symmetrieebene wirkt ein: A stroke on the symmetry plane acts once, not twice.
Ein Zug bewegt nur Punkte, die dem Pinse: A stroke only moves points that face the brush.
Ein Zug hat die Fläche durch die Wand da: A stroke pushed the surface through the wall behind it, so the spot prints open or doubled.
Ein Zug hat die Wand dünner gemacht, als: A stroke made the wall thinner than this material prints reliably. Adding material there helps.
Ein Zylinder, um das Spiel dünner als di: A cylinder, thinner than the hole by the clearance, without head or thread.
Ein anderer Lauf hat die gemeinsame Graf: Another task did not release the shared graphics card within the waiting period. Let it finish and try again.
Ein anderer Update-Vorgang benutzt den Z: Another update process is using the cache.
Ein anderes Programm auf demselben Rechn:
Another program on the same computer may operate Solidon, an AI assistant such as Claude Code for example; the connection is called MCP.

**It is off until you switch it on**, in the settings, together with the port. Solidon then listens only on `127.0.0.1` and cannot be reached from any other computer. In the other program, `http://127.0.0.1:8787/mcp` is entered as the server.

**What comes in is a transaction like any other:** the history shows it with a note that it came from outside, and Ctrl+Z takes it back. Nothing that looks like a file path gets through, because an outside program should not decide what is read here.
Ein anderes Programm auf diesem Rechner: Another program on this machine may call the same operations as the menus. Over 127.0.0.1 only, and Ctrl+Z undoes every call.
Ein anderes Programm bedient Solidon, lo: Another program operates Solidon, locally, with an off switch, and every step can be undone.
Ein anderes SDXL-Modell geht auch: Solid: Another SDXL model works too: Solidon takes what lies in the folder, preferring *juggernaut* and *dreamshaper* over the base model. Models with *refiner*, *inpaint* or *turbo* in the name are not taken — they do a different job.
Ein benanntes Maß des Projekts einsetzen: Insert a named dimension of the project — changed in one place.
Ein benanntes Merkmal des Rezepts ist un: A named feature of the recipe is invalid.
Ein benanntes Merkmal gibt es im Ergebni: A named feature no longer exists in the result. Rename the recipe's features, or remove the entry.
Ein benanntes Merkmal ist nach dieser Op: A named feature can no longer be found after this operation.
Ein druckbares Innengewinde in eine vorh: Put a printable internal thread into an existing hole.
Ein durchgehender Kanal trägt Rippen auf: A through passage carries ribs on the same axis.
Ein eigener Baustein ließ sich nicht lad: One of your own parts could not be loaded.
Ein eigenes Rezept ließ sich nicht laden: One of your recipes could not be loaded.
Ein erkanntes Gerät braucht Zugriff durc: Solidon needs access to a detected device; this explains how to grant it.
Ein erzeugter Versuch ist noch nicht im: One generated attempt is not in the project yet and will be lost on closing.
Ein extern erzeugtes GLB oder STL bearbe: You edit an externally generated GLB or STL like any other body. “Generate model” creates models through a local ComfyUI.
Ein externes Programm hat nicht geantwor: An external program did not answer.
Ein festgeschriebener Stand dieser Sitzu: A locked-in state of this session. Once set, the result comes from there and no longer from the strokes — they remain as a record but no longer take effect.
Ein flacher Rand am Teil — mehr Haftfläc: A flat rim around the part — more grip area, peeled off after printing.
Ein freigegebener Parameter steht nicht: An exposed parameter is not part of the selection. Create it in the project before exposing it.
Ein freigegebenes Maß des Rezepts ist un: A shared dimension in the recipe is invalid.
Ein freigegebenes Maß verweist auf keine: An exposed dimension refers to no project parameter.
Ein gedruckter Fuß, oder die Tasche für: A printed foot, or the pocket for a bought rubber one.
Ein gedrucktes Floß unter dem Teil — bes: A printed raft under the part — best adhesion, costs time and a clean underside.
Ein gelesenes Muster, das Solidon nicht: A pattern read from the model that Solidon does not draw itself. Choose one of the eight styles and it is redrawn in that style.
Ein gemessener Wert kann hier nicht nega: A measured value cannot be negative here.
Ein geschlossener gezeichneter Verlauf b: A closed drawn path forms the centreline of the gasket ring.
Ein geschlossener gezeichneter Verlauf o: A closed drawn path or an explicitly selected opening.
Ein glatter Stift gehört in eine Bohrung: A plain pin belongs in a hole, not in a thread. Choose the shape “To fit the hole”.
Ein gleichmäßiger Bogen aus Radius und W: An even arc from radius and angle — the pipe bend, without a drawing.
Ein hingelegter Körper braucht mehr Fläc: A body laid down needs more area than a standing one. Off means each stays where it stood — even when it then sits inside its neighbour.
Ein kegeliges Gewinde lässt sich hier we: A tapered thread can be neither changed nor removed here. Choose another feature.
Ein linksgängiges Gewinde lässt sich hie: A left-hand thread cannot be recut here. Insert it again as a part.
Ein massiver Klotz verbraucht Material,: A solid block uses material nobody sees. This project splits it and hollows out both halves.
Ein mehrgängiges Gewinde hat kein Gegens: A multi-start thread has no counterpart in the library — its threads are single-start.
Ein mehrgängiges Gewinde lässt sich hier: A multi-start thread cannot be recut here. Insert it again as a part.
Ein mitgedrucktes Scharnier verbindet De: A printed-in-place hinge joins the lid and container.
Ein mitgereistes Rezept ließ sich nicht: A recipe that came with the file could not be imported.
Ein offener Befund — anklicken öffnet de: One open finding — click to open the report.
Ein offener Kanal hat keine Länge innen: An open channel has no inner length — it runs to its ends. Change the width or the depth.
Ein rechteckiges Musterfeld oder die gan: A rectangular pattern area or the entire selected face up to its edges. Holes remain open.
Ein runder Rand wie die Mündung einer Bo: A round rim, such as the mouth of a hole, only counts as horizontal, top or bottom when it lies flat. Eine STL-Datei enthält nur Dreiecke, kei:
An STL file contains only triangles, no hole and no dimension. Solidon reads the shapes back: after loading, a recognition fits cylinders, cones, spheres, rings and roundings into the faces. Whatever fits becomes a **feature** with a centre, an axis, a size and an ID that stays. The hole is a hole again.

**Thirteen kinds, and the name tells the position:**

* **Hole**: a cylinder that goes in, numbered as “Hole 1”, “Hole 2”.
* **Slot**: two round ends and two straight flanks, with width and length.
* **Pattern**: many identical cells on a face, the way *Apply texture* draws them. A honeycomb holder with 196 cells is one feature with spacing, cell width and depth; *Change feature* sets them anew, *Remove feature* fills the cells. A small field that shows only as single features: select them in the object tree and use *Combine into a pattern*.
* **Peg**: a cylinder that sticks out.
* **Countersink** or **Taper**: a cone, inwards or outwards.
* **Socket** or **Dome**: a spherical face.
* **Groove** or **Bead**: a ring running around.
* **Concave fillet** or **Fillet**: a rounded edge.
* **Internal thread** or **External thread**.
* **Air pocket**: a cavity with no way out. Whether it is intended, say as a pocket for a magnet, only whoever drew the part knows.
* **Open edge**: a hole in the mesh that wants repairing.
* **Face**, named after its direction: “Top”, “Front”, “Right side”. A wall facing inwards is called “Top inside”.
* **Curved face**: a bent piece of surface without a plane of its own, such as the bowl of a D. You can drill on it, place primitives and parts, and assign a separate filament. To draw, choose a flat face or a sketch plane.

Where two names are given, the direction decides: concave fillet inside, fillet outside. In the object tree, the features sit under their body, similar ones grouped together.

**Not every shape becomes a feature.** Recognition needs sufficiently precise and unambiguous geometry. Its minimum sizes are not general printing limits. On freeform surfaces, it omits spheres, rings, cones and fillets that lack reliable evidence; holes, pegs, faces and threads remain. The report lists omitted round shapes. A complete sphere or ring can still be recognised.

**The same shape in a different position.** A part you move or rotate in Solidon keeps its features and their IDs. If the same part is imported again in a different position, a shape right at the limit of recognition, such as a very shallow arc or a short piece of a cone, may appear as a feature one time and not the next. The same can happen between computers with different processors.

## The Selection tab

Click something, in the view or in the object tree, and you find it on the right under *Selection*; the click brings that tab to the front. At the top is what is selected, for example “Hole 1”, and below it, for a hole, its size and the standard size: 5.19 mm is the clearance hole for M5. Below are the actions, each a group of fields.

**The fields hold the measured values**, because a changed number is the operation. To have the hole two millimetres further right, change exactly that number. As soon as typing pauses briefly, the view shows the preview. *Apply* at the bottom runs the action whose fields you touched last, and the line above it says which one that is. Only then does a step appear in the history.

**Rather point than type?** *Set in the view* above *Apply* gives the hole a handle in the view to move and turn it, knobs to pull and dimension lines to two edges of the face; every dimension can also be typed there. A slot you pull keeps its shape. *Apply* turns it into a step, *Cancel* or Escape discards it.

**An empty coordinate field means: the hole stays where it is.** In *Change bore* and *Pull into a slot*, X, Y and Z are set to “as measured”. A number you enter is a new position, zero included; that is how a hole ends up exactly in the middle of the part.

**There are six actions**, depending on the kind:

* *Move feature*: the new centre as X, Y, Z.
* *Change bore* or *Change feature*: the new diameter, for a hole including the material tolerance; for a slot the width, and the ends grow with it.
* *Pull into a slot*: length and direction. On a round hole, the length starts at twice its diameter, so the screw has one diameter of travel. A slot can be lengthened or shortened and keeps its direction until you change it. The material tolerance widens the slot, the screw's travel stays as entered.
* *Turn feature*: axis and angle.
* *Duplicate feature*: the same hole a second time somewhere else.
* *Remove feature*: no field, *Apply* is enough.

Hole and slot can do all six, a peg everything except pulling. A spherical face can be neither turned nor pulled. A cone can do everything except pulling while it stands on its own; above a hole it cannot be moved by itself. A fillet changes its radius or disappears completely, also in an imported model. An air pocket can be moved and removed; removed, it is filled with material. A thread changes its diameter and pitch or is removed completely; it cannot be moved, turned or duplicated. Face, curved face, open edge and ring have none of these actions.

**What is not possible is said in a sentence**, not shown as a grey field; on a ring, for example, the way via the whole body or a ring used as a tool.

**Several features of the same kind on one body** give every action a checkbox such as “Apply to all 4 of the same kind”. Four holes in a row are thus drilled out in one step, and one Ctrl+Z takes all four back.

**On a face**, none of the six actions applies. That is where the parts attach, and the *Parts* button opens the catalogue.

**An edge is the third thing a click can hit.** The first click selects the body, the second the edge. On the right you then find *Fillet*, *Add a chamfer* and *Add bead*, each with one dimension. This works on an imported model too; there the rounding is made of straight pieces finer than a nozzle can resolve. For all vertical edges, choose the group in the dialog instead of each edge. *Offset face* and *Apply draft angle* also work on the imported mesh.

**Two marked features show their distance**, centre to centre and per axis in X, Y and Z. It is information, with no button and no step in the history. With three marked, the tab stays as it was.

## What else you can do with a feature

**Del hits the feature, not the body.** With a hole selected, the key takes the hole away; with no feature selected, it deletes every marked object.

**The handle sits on the selected feature.** Select a hole and call up *Move*, and you find it at the hole's opening. A drag on it becomes *Move feature* or *Turn feature*, and the part stays put. There is no scaling cube there; a hole grows through its diameter. While you drag, a cylinder shows where it is going; the body only changes when you let go.

**When moving, the ID travels along.** A fit that points at this hole keeps its reference. A copy made with *Duplicate feature* gets an ID of its own.

**Three warnings can come up:** a through hole that no longer goes through after moving; a slot that sticks out over the edge at one end, even if its centre sits in the material; and a countersink above a hole that cannot be moved on its own because it runs into the hole. The message names the way: select the feature in the middle, or fill the hole and create both anew, *Countersink* being an operation of its own.

**What the recognition found** is shown by the *Features* map under *Analysis*, before you click.

**Changing hole and lead-in together.** In *Change bore*, *Include countersink, steps and narrowing* changes all diameters together, including the opening of a narrowing; lead-in width, countersink angle and step depths stay. *Hole diameter only* leaves countersink and steps as they are. One Ctrl+Z takes the change back.

**Recognising one spot on purpose.** If a feature is missing on a large mesh, right-click the surface, choose *Detect features here*, enlarge the radius until the feature is fully covered and open it from the list with *Edit feature …*. After the preview, Solidon applies recognition and change together, and one Ctrl+Z takes both back. *Apply features only* stores just the recognition.

Setting a hexagon so deep into a wall that an M4 nut fits and the screw still bites is half an hour of work the first time. A part does it: click the face or hole, choose the part, choose the size. [Your first part](manual:first-part) shows the way in pictures.

**After inserting, the part stands in the view**, on the selected face, in the selected hole or on top of the body, with dimension lines to the edges and a handle. Dragging or a click on another spot moves it, and the dimensions can be typed too. Only *Apply* inserts it; Escape goes back to the values. With no body selected, *Insert* stays locked and says why on the button; you can still browse the catalogue.

**The dimensions come from a table.** Across-flats of the M4 nut, seat of the heat-set insert, width of the living hinge are looked up, not guessed.

**Nut trap**: the pocket for a hex nut that is dropped in during printing. The most common way to a thread that takes load.

![](figure:part-nut-trap)

**Heat-set insert**: the stepped hole for a brass insert that is melted in with a soldering iron. More work, but it can be undone as often as you like.

![](figure:part-heatset)

**Latch**: a springy arm that gives way when joining and then snaps in. A lid that holds without a screw.

![](figure:part-snap-fit)

**Living hinge**: a spot so thin that it bends instead of breaking. The joint is printed along with the part.

![](figure:part-hinge)

**Pegboard hook**: one to six hooks in the grid of a SKÅDIS pegboard, a back plate on request. In from above through the slots, then pull down; a springy latch tongue holds the part even when someone pulls on it. If you take it off often, switch the tongue off. It is printed lying down, so that the tongue flexes across its layers.

![](figure:part-pegboard-hook)

**Hinge eye**: a lug with a hole. Two of them and a dowel pin make a joint that turns.

![](figure:part-hinge-eye)

**Barrel hinge**: two lugs around a printed pin, movable straight off the plate. The gap between them is the fit, and *Clearance* sets it.

**Corner gusset**: the triangle in an inside corner that holds two walls at a right angle. For a single floppy wall, there is the stiffening rib.

![](figure:part-gusset)

**Foot**: a printed foot or the pocket for a rubber foot. The chamfer points down so that the elephant foot of the first layer squeezes into nothing.

![](figure:part-foot)

**Cable clip**: a bracket whose opening is narrower than the cable. It guides but does not hold against pulling; that is what the cable gland is for.

![](figure:part-cable-clip)

**Printable thread**: an internal thread or a threaded stud for a printed counterpart, not for a metal screw. With the Internal thread box ticked, it cuts its own hole in a face. Besides the M sizes, *Custom size* takes any diameter, for a pipe for example. In an existing hole it sets the thread that fits, see [A thread in a hole](manual:thread-a-hole).

Add to these the screw hole, magnet pocket, cable gland, rib, keyhole, insert ball bearing, screw, printed nut, T-slot tongue, wall mount, snap fit, dowel pin and bore, snap connector for a seam, tab with hole, pipe clamp, the U-shaped, round, fork and shelf holders and the test bodies from [Trying instead of guessing: variants and calibration](manual:variants). The catalogue sorts them into groups, each with a picture.

![](figure:catalog)

**A part stays changeable** like every operation: it is in the history, and the spots where it attaches keep their names.

**Two parts that belong together are made together.** *Set counterparts …* under *Create → Parts*: mark the spot on each of the two parts, choose the pair, enter the dimensions once. Solidon places both halves, enters the fit and puts everything into one step. There are three pairs: dowel pin and bore, printed screw and nut, heat-set insert and clearance hole. If one of the two spots is a thread, there is nothing to choose: the matching counter-thread appears on the other part.

**Dividing an organizer.** Open *Create → Basic shapes → Create organizer*, enter the dimensions and choose *Arrange compartments …*. *Keep outer dimensions* or *Keep clear compartment dimensions* decides whether the drawer has to fit or the contents. Select a compartment or a divider in the top view or in the tree, change compartment sizes and wall heights, and the preview follows. *Apply layout* takes you back to the dialog, *Apply* creates the part, and in the history the layout can be reopened later. Tray, divider, rim and plug-in foot also exist as separate parts.

**Way 1: adapt someone else's model.** Downloaded, almost fits: import, repair, drill, export. The most common way; [Check and print a model](manual:print-a-model) and [Drill a hole](manual:drill-a-hole) show how it goes.

Für den Umriss, den kein Grundkörper her:
For the outline no basic shape can give you, such as a base plate with a cut-out for a power supply.

**It starts at the top in the toolbar.** *Draw* swings the view square onto the drawing plane, and you draw in the model. What it becomes, you decide at the end. Escape gets you out again.

![](figure:sketch-mode)

**First the plane.** *XY* lies flat like the print bed, *XZ* and *YZ* stand upright, and the flat faces of existing bodies are in the list too. The sentence beside it says how the print layers lie relative to the drawing: parallel on *XY*, across on the upright planes, and there a horizontal line later becomes a seam. It is quicker with a right-click on a face, in the view or in the object tree: *Draw on this face*. Under *New plane …* you create a plane offset in parallel, tilted about an axis or through three points; the distance may be a project parameter, and the plane moves with its face.

**Tools and keys:** Line `L`, Rectangle `R`, Circle `C`, Arc `A`, Point `P`, Curve `S`, Polygon `V`, Slot `G`, Trim `T`. Polygon, slot, bolt circle and hole grid take two clicks: centre and corner, the centres of the two round ends, centre and first hole, two opposite holes. Number of corners, width, count or hole diameter are next to it in the bar. The line continues as a chain; a curve ends with a double-click, Enter or a click on its last point. `1`, `2` and `3` switch between XY, XZ and YZ; `Esc` cancels an element you have started and switches to selecting. Everything is created as a drawing with constraints and stays dimensionable.

**Looking and dragging.** You move the view as in the main window, and *Fit to view* (`Home`) brings everything into view. With *Select*, a drag moves a point, and whatever hangs on it follows. **Ctrl while clicking collects**: *Parallel* and *Perpendicular* need two lines, *Symmetric* two points and an axis, and the order of the clicks counts. `Del` deletes the selection together with its constraints, in the constraint list only the entry. `Ctrl+Z` here undoes the last change on the sheet, not the last step in the history.

**Snapping.** A click near an existing point snaps to it, and both get the *Connected* constraint: they stay together even if something else moves later. Where no point is nearby, *Snap to grid* snaps it to the nearest grid line. Its spacing follows the zoom in steps of 1, 2, 5; a spacing you type in stays, and *Automatic* makes it follow the zoom again.

**Dimensioning while drawing.** With line and circle, a dimension field appears at the pointer after the first click: type a length or a diameter, press Enter. The direction comes from the pointer, the number stays as a constraint. Ø or R next to the field swaps diameter for radius, in every circle field of the application. Afterwards, `D` dimensions two selected points, also with an expression: `@breite/2` ties the dimension to a project parameter.

**Constraints hold the drawing together.** Select something, then press the button or right-click on the spot. These include: distance, radius, diameter, angle, connected, horizontal, vertical, parallel, perpendicular, tangent, on curve, curvature continuous, equal, midpoint, concentric, symmetric, fixed and a reference dimension that only measures. Only what suits the selection is offered, and a second click on the pressed button removes the constraint. On the right are the constraints of the selected line or point, with their total above. Two that contradict each other are always shown. Hover over an entry and the points it holds light up. A right-click on a point shows what hangs on it and removes it one by one.

![](figure:sketch-editor)

**At the bottom it says how firm the drawing is.** *Fully defined* means nothing moves any more. “4 more dimensions and nothing can move” means the sketch can still be shifted; it works all the same. If two dimensions contradict each other, Solidon names them, and the last valid position stays.

**Changing without drawing again:** *Trim* cuts away the half you click, *Extend* lets it grow, *Offset* (`O`) puts a contour at a distance beside it, negative inwards, *Mirror* mirrors the selection about the X or Y axis. *Guide line* (`X`) carries constraints but forms no profile, for example as a centre line. *Project* brings the edges of existing bodies that cut this plane into the drawing, *Face outline* the edge of the face with its holes. Both arrive fixed and as guide lines: that is how you align to an imported part instead of measuring. It is a copy; if the body changes, it does not follow.

**The edge of the build volume is drawn dashed.** Draw beyond it and the line says: *the sketch extends beyond it*. For small parts it lies outside the view.

![](figure:sketch-uses)

**Finally you say what it becomes.** *Pull up* and *Carve* are right at the finished contour. *Done* unfolds all kinds, each with a sentence: pull up, cut in as a pocket, cut a hole pattern, revolve about the vertical axis, sweep along an arc or span between two outlines. What does not work says why. *Discard* leaves the mode, and the status line names the way back.

![](figure:sketch-result)

**The drawing stays a value in the history.** A double-click on the step reopens the drawing directly. A moved line recomputes the operation, and the rest of the project stays. A drawn circle becomes a round cylinder, not a polygon.

**Using an existing drawing.** Drag an SVG or DXF file into the window. Under *Extrude a drawing* you choose the contours in the list or in the preview, *All valid* marks every usable one; inner rings stay holes. Set height and width and check the preview. Contours that cannot be used stay visible with a reason. Later, the step in the history reopens *Choose contours …*, and height and width are then in the operation dialog.

Ist das Teil zu groß für den Bauraum, wi:
If the part is too big for the build volume, it is split, and the halves have to come back together.

**The shortest way** is the *Split* tool in the tool strip (Alt+7). Two clicks on the part draw a line, and it is split there, straight into the screen. *Prepare for plugging together* is ticked from the start: pins in one half, matching holes in the other. Next to it you choose what holds them:

* **Round** prints cleanest but needs two, otherwise the halves twist.
* **Hexagon** already holds against twisting on its own.
* **Dovetail** also holds against pulling apart across the seam, because it is narrower at the back than at the front.
* **Snap** clicks in, with a spring arm in one half and a pocket with a catch in the other. It holds without glue and comes apart again, but needs a seam of at least 5.4 mm; if it is narrower, round pins are used, and the report says why.

**Split automatically …** on the right for the selected body also finds the spot, using the same layer analysis as the search for the best position. What weighs most is that the seam is one contour rather than several thin webs. After that come an even cross-section, which glues more cleanly than a slope, a free thinnest spot, halves of similar size and finally which pieces need fewer supports.

**If a part needs several cuts, the search plans the whole sequence**, by the number of pieces and glue joints at the end. A mirror-symmetric part is split in its plane of symmetry, and both sides then print with the same settings. Loose pieces are separated at the gap, without seam or pin.

![](figure:split)

**Every cut face gets two dowel pins**, so that nothing twists. The diameter comes from the face, the clearance from the calibrated material profile, and every pin is a fit that is checked at every evaluation.

**Every cut is an operation of its own**: the plane stays a number you can move, and Ctrl+Z takes back one cut, not the whole split. To type the plane, use *Split at a plane* on the right for the selected body, with axis and position; zero pins there means just cutting.

**The pieces are named for what they are:** “… A · Pins” and “… B · Holes”. When *Split automatically* makes three or more pieces, it counts them: “… 1 of 3 · Pins”, “… 2 of 3 · Pins and holes”, “… 3 of 3 · Holes”. When exporting, the file name tells you which part you are holding.

Jede Operation steht im Verlauf und blei:
Every operation sits in the history and stays changeable there. A model here is the list of steps it came from, not just a mesh of triangles.

![](figure:stack)

**A double-click on a step** reopens it with the values stored in the file. To move a hole, change the number; only what depends on it is computed again. Ctrl+Z takes this change back too. [Drill a hole](manual:drill-a-hole) shows it with an example.

**“Edit this step”** is also on the feature, in the context menu of the view and in the object tree: the way from the result back to its step, without hunting for the line in the history. Whatever a part created, the object tree groups under that part's name.

**Select several steps** with Ctrl or Shift. Exactly these go into a part of your own ([Your own parts](manual:own-parts)); with no selection, the whole history counts.

**Deleting** is in the context menu of the list and in the bar below it, and it can be undone. Because a deleted step hits the steps built on it, this is the one place in the history where Solidon asks first; the question names the affected steps and the way back with Ctrl+Z.

**Undo takes back a whole transaction**, never half a step. A proposal from the chat is exactly one transaction.

**Two limits are deliberate.** Undone steps are dropped as soon as a new one comes; there are no branches. And a change that alters the number of objects while later steps work with them is refused, because the new bodies are not the old ones.

**Clicking sets things up.** Select a face and then call an operation, and position and axis are already filled in, the size is not: a countersink takes the screw head, not the diameter of the hole beneath it. On a clicked hole, the dialog names the matching standard size and asks where none fits, instead of inventing one.

After that, STEP works and holes, edges and faces can be edited; it has no construction history. Whatever lies on no recognised face stays flat triangles; the report names the share and the deviation.

Some shapes cannot be dimensioned: a handle that should sit well in the hand, a figure, a grown transition. That is what the brush is for.

**Three stages, and the second is easily skipped.** First a rough shape from basic shapes, blended softly (*Blend together* on the right once the bodies are selected). Then *Even out the triangles*, so that the points are spread evenly everywhere. Then *Sculpt*. Without the second stage the mesh cannot follow the brush, and the bar says so.

**The whole session is one step in the history**, not every stroke, because a figure has thousands. During the session Ctrl+Z takes back a stroke, afterwards the whole session.

**Six tools.** *Add* and *Carve* are the same with the opposite sign. *Smooth*, *Inflate* and *Flatten* each need one more pass, and the bar shows how many. *Pinch* pulls towards the middle of the stroke and makes edges.

**Within one stage the order does not matter:** two strokes over the same spot add up on the starting surface. With *Start afresh*, the next stroke builds on what is already there. If a stroke reaches into a hollow that an earlier stroke dug, it starts afresh there by itself and digs deeper.

**Symmetry can be changed afterwards**, even on a finished session. It mirrors about the centre of the body as it stands before the strokes; it stays put while you sculpt. A stroke on the mirror plane acts once, not twice.

**The brush only affects the side facing it.** The underside of a thin plate or the inner wall of a hollow body stays where it is.

**When not to use it:** on a part that is still being dimensioned, because a stroke sits at a spot in space and loses its surface when the shape beneath it changes. For a transition between two bodies, *Blend together* is better, three numbers instead of a hundred strokes.

**In return, the wall thickness is tracked:** spots that are too thin appear as a number in the bar before the slicer finds them. If a stroke pierces the wall or leaves less than the minimum wall, the report says so afterwards and shows the spot.
Some shapes cannot be dimensioned. Way 4 builds the form from primitives and shapes it with the brush.

Ob ein Modell druckbar ist, sieht man ih:
You can rarely tell by looking whether a model will print: the thinnest wall, the overhang, the island that starts in mid-air. Five tools below the view show it, and none of them changes the model. You cannot break anything with them.

**Measure** shows the distance between two points; the pointer snaps to corners and edges. While you measure, the view drops its perspective so that you do not aim past the point. A click on a face measures the **wall thickness** behind it. Every distance stays as a dimension until you remove it, so several can be compared.

**Section** lays a plane through the model, and the slider pulls it through. The cut face is drawn closed, so a cavity shows as a cavity.

**Analysis** colours the model by one of seven maps. **Wall thickness**, **Overhang**, **Support needed** and **Curvature** tell whether it will print. **Mesh defects** shows open edges, places where more than two faces meet and faces that cut into each other; that is usually the reason when uniting or subtracting fails. **Features** shows what the recognition found, **Fits** which faces take part in a fit and which of them is violated. The legend always gives the range of values and where they come from. A click on a warning in the report flies the camera to the spot.

**Layers** shows the model as it falls apart into layers; with several bodies, pick one first. The slider runs through it, and beside it are the layer number and total, the Z height, the cross-section area, the number of islands and the overhang area. The legend tells contour, island and overhang apart by more than colour. This is Solidon's own layer analysis, not the slicer's computation; the two sets of numbers are kept apart.

![](figure:layers)

**Exploded** pulls several bodies apart for viewing. Export and history stay untouched.

**The shadow tells you something too.** It falls for every piece separately, and a part that has fallen apart into several pieces casts several shadows.
